previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, and a history of dialysis line infections was admitted from a nursing home with weakness, hypotension, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Initial imaging suggested acute cholecystitis, but her pain resolved quickly and prior scans were similar, leading the surgical team to attribute her discomfort to constipation. Blood cultures revealed high-grade MRSA bacteremia, prompting concern for a dialysis line infection. The existing tunnelled line was changed over a wire, but due to pus at the site, it was later removed and replaced with a temporary right-sided line, which was then converted to a new tunnelled catheter. Surveillance cultures remained negative, and a transesophageal echocardiogram showed no endocarditis. She completed a two-week course of vancomycin, initiated from the date of the new line placement. Her blood pressure improved with fluid removal via dialysis, allowing discontinuation of metoprolol, and her insulin dose was reduced due to stable glucose control. She was discharged to extended care with plans to complete antibiotics, continue warfarin, and monitor INR and blood sugar.
